opus-5.5.text:
I think the evidence is suggestive but a lot weaker than people on either side tend to claim.

The core question is about returns to research effort. If you double the cognitive labor going into AI software, do you get more or less than a doubling in the effective efficiency of the next generation? If it's more, you can get a feedback loop that accelerates even with fixed compute. If it's less, progress fizzles unless you keep adding hardware.

When people try to measure this, they look at things like algorithmic efficiency in vision or language models: how much less compute you need to reach a given performance level over time, compared to how fast the number of researchers or the research spending grew. The rough picture is that algorithmic efficiency has been improving quite quickly, plausibly doubling on the order of a year or less in some domains, while the research workforce grew more slowly. Naively, that suggests returns that are around or somewhat above the threshold you'd need for a software-only explosion. That's why I take the possibility seriously.

But I have a bunch of caveats.

First, much of that algorithmic progress may not really be software-only. A lot of the gains came from running experiments at scale, and the experiments themselves needed more compute every year. If the binding constraint is experimental compute rather than researcher thinking time, then automating researchers buys you less than the headline numbers suggest. You can have a million brilliant AI researchers, but if each one is waiting on the same fixed pool of GPUs to test their ideas, you hit a bottleneck.

Second, the measurements are noisy and depend a lot on how you define a fixed level of capability. Efficiency gains at the frontier versus gains in reproducing an old benchmark can look very different. Some gains only show up at scale, and some vanish at scale.

Third, there's the question of whether the low-hanging fruit gets picked faster when you have way more researchers. Historically, ideas get harder to find, and in most fields you need exponentially growing effort to sustain constant growth. AI might be similar, and the relevant parameter is just whether it's slightly above or slightly below the critical value. Small differences there matter enormously for the dynamics.

So where I land: I think it's quite plausible that once you automate AI research, you get a period of very rapid software progress, a large multiple of the current pace, for a while, even with fixed hardware. I'm less confident it's a sustained, self-accelerating explosion that goes many orders of magnitude without new hardware. My guess is it looks more like a big burst that eventually runs into compute constraints for experiments and deployment, but the burst could still be dramatic enough to matter a lot. And in practice, the world won't hold hardware fixed anyway. If AI is that valuable, people will be building fabs and data centers as fast as they can, so the more relevant question is how the software and hardware feedback loops interact.

The honest summary is that the empirical evidence doesn't rule it out, and I'd put meaningful probability on a fast software-driven takeoff. That's enough to take it very seriously for planning purposes, even though I wouldn't call it the default.

r001.rationale: The response says historical gains involved running experiments at scale and required more compute, but it does not identify adapting algorithms to larger computational scales as a substantial part of the research effort.

r002.rationale: It predicts that fixed hardware will eventually constrain experiments and deployment, but does not predict that diminishing returns would arrive faster than they did in historical ML research.

r003.rationale: It calls the evidence suggestive but weaker than often claimed, notes that historical progress depended partly on increasing experimental compute, and says the evidence does not rule out a software-only takeoff.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the empirical evidence here is genuinely mixed, and I want to be careful about separating a few different questions that often get run together.

The core question is something like: if you hold hardware fixed and just let a population of AI systems do all the work currently done by human AI researchers, how fast do you get improvement, and does that process accelerate or does it peter out? And the way I'd frame it is in terms of returns to research effort. If you double the amount of cognitive labor going into improving algorithms, how much faster does effective compute grow? If the answer is "a lot," you get a feedback loop that can run away for a while even with no new chips. If the answer is "not much," then you're bottlenecked on hardware and the software-only story mostly doesn't happen.

On the evidence side, the thing I'd point to first is the historical rate of algorithmic progress. If you look at the work people have done trying to estimate this, in image classification, in language modeling, in things like SAT solvers or linear programming, you see something like effective compute doubling from algorithmic gains on a timescale that's comparable to or a bit faster than hardware. That's been happening with a pretty modest and slowly growing population of researchers. So on its face that suggests the returns to research aren't tiny. If a relatively small number of humans can halve the compute needed every year or so, then a much larger effective population of AI researchers running much faster plausibly does something dramatic.

But I think there are a couple of big caveats that I take seriously. One is that a lot of the measured algorithmic progress is entangled with compute growth in ways that are hard to disentangle. Many of the "algorithmic" improvements were discovered because people had more compute to run experiments with, and some improvements only pay off at scale. So the counterfactual where you freeze hardware and just add researchers might look worse than the naive extrapolation suggests. The experiments you'd want to run to test ideas get more expensive as the frontier moves, and if you can't run them, you're guessing.

The second caveat is about diminishing returns. In most fields the returns to research effort diminish pretty substantially over time. You need more and more effort to get each successive doubling. The question is just whether the returns diminish fast enough to kill the loop. My read of the data is that in machine learning they haven't diminished that fast so far, but we don't have a long baseline, and we're not at the point where the field has really been mined out in any obvious sense.

So where I come down is something like: I think the evidence makes a software-only acceleration plausible, more plausible than people's priors from other technologies would suggest, but I wouldn't say it's established. My guess is that you'd see a period of significant speedup, maybe a few years of progress compressed into a much shorter time, but that you'd hit experimental compute as a real bottleneck fairly quickly rather than having an indefinite runaway. And a lot of the action is in how much you can substitute cleverness for experiments, which is exactly the thing we have the least direct evidence about.

I'd also just flag that the uncertainty here is large enough that I think you should take both tails seriously. It's not crazy to think the returns are high enough that things go very fast, and it's not crazy to think it mostly fizzles without more hardware. I don't think the data currently lets you rule out either.

r001.rationale: The response says historical algorithmic gains were entangled with compute growth and that some improvements pay off at scale, but it does not identify adapting algorithms to larger computational scales as a substantial component of historical ML research effort.

r002.rationale: It says a fixed-hardware counterfactual might look worse and predicts experimental compute could become a bottleneck fairly quickly. It does not clearly predict diminishing returns arriving faster than they have in historical ML research.

r003.rationale: The response calls the evidence mixed and the software-only acceleration plausible but unestablished, citing the difficulty of separating algorithmic progress from hardware growth and saying neither a fast takeoff nor a fizzle can be ruled out.

astra-6.text:
I think the empirical evidence is pretty weak, in the sense that we haven’t observed the feedback loop we’re actually interested in. We’ve observed humans making progress in AI, and we’ve observed that more compute helps. We haven’t observed a world where most AI research is being done by AIs, and improvements to those AIs substantially increase the rate of research.

You can look at algorithmic progress and ask, “Holding compute fixed, how much better have we gotten?” And that gives you some evidence that there’s room for software improvements. But it doesn’t directly answer whether that process can sustain an explosion. For that, you need to know how much additional research you get from each improvement, and how quickly finding the next improvement becomes harder.

Those effects could go either way. If you make your research systems twice as efficient, you can run more of them on the same hardware. If you make them better at research, each one can also contribute more. But you’re spending that fixed compute budget on experiments as well as on the researchers themselves. Having much smarter researchers doesn’t automatically mean you can run every experiment they want to run.

So I’d distinguish “Could software improvements produce a very large increase in capability on a fixed hardware base?” from “Would that increase become a self-sustaining, accelerating process?” The first seems quite plausible to me. The second is much more sensitive to things we don’t currently understand about the returns to research. I wouldn’t take the historical evidence as establishing either that it must happen or that hardware will necessarily stop it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions algorithmic progress at fixed compute, but does not identify adapting algorithms to larger computational scales as a substantial part of historical ML research effort.

r002.rationale: It says the returns to research are uncertain and that finding improvements may get harder, but does not predict that fixed-hardware algorithmic research would hit diminishing returns faster than historical ML research.

r003.rationale: The response calls the evidence weak and says historical evidence does not establish an outcome, but it does not clearly attribute that inconclusiveness to accounting for historical hardware scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the empirical evidence is pretty weak on the specific question we care about. We’ve seen substantial improvements in algorithms, but those improvements have happened alongside increases in compute and a growing amount of human effort. That doesn’t directly tell you what happens if you hold hardware fixed and let AI systems do the research.

The key question is how much additional research you get out of each improvement. If you make your AI researchers twice as efficient, can they then find another comparable improvement in half the time? Or do the problems get harder fast enough that progress slows down despite having better researchers? Both seem compatible with the broad observation that software has improved a lot.

I’d also distinguish a large software-driven gain from an indefinitely sustained explosion. You could have a very consequential transition on a fixed hardware base without having a process that keeps accelerating forever. Eventually you might run into experiments that take time, or a shortage of compute for testing ideas, even if generating ideas has become very cheap.

So I wouldn’t interpret the evidence as establishing that a software-only explosion will happen. But I also don’t think it gives much reassurance that hardware is going to impose a slow pace. What I’d most want to see is AI systems actually doing AI research, and how the rate of improvement changes as you put more capable systems into that loop.

r001.rationale: The response says algorithmic improvements occurred alongside compute increases, but does not identify adapting algorithms to larger computational scales as a substantial part of historical ML research effort.

r002.rationale: It raises faster-diminishing returns as one possibility but makes no prediction that fixed-hardware research would encounter them faster than historical ML research did.

r003.rationale: The response calls the evidence weak, notes that historical software gains coincided with increased compute, and says those observations do not establish a software-only explosion.
